original.source: Every number computed in Step 1 is a coefficient in front of a local functional, and its sign and normalisation are inherited from three classical data: the odd pairing on the fields, the BV action and the linear differential $Q$. The sources supply the ten-dimensional action [ESW, (31)] and its dimensional reduction [ESW, Prop 2.20, §10.3], while the pairing on the antifields stays implicit in the phrase "natural $(-1)$-shifted symplectic structure" [ESW, Def 1.34]. This chapter fixes all three data for the reduction to Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$, writes the interaction vertex by vertex, and shows that the classical master equation determines the relative signs of the pairing.

where $V$ is the complexification of $\mathbb R^4$ (the directions of spacetime) and $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ consists of the six transverse directions. In the notation of [ESW, §2.6] the ten-dimensional space is $V_{\mathbb R}$ and the four-dimensional subspace is $W_{\mathbb R}$; here $W$ alone denotes the multiplicity space of [ESW, §10].

• $\mathfrak g$ is the complexified gauge Lie algebra, with bracket $[-,-]$ and a nondegenerate invariant symmetric pairing $(-,-)$, positive definite on the compact real form [ESW, §3.1]. The coupling constant sits in $(-,-)$. The inverse pairing is the element $(-,-)^{-1}\in\mathfrak g\otimes\mathfrak g$.

• $q\colon\wedge^\bullet V_{10}\to\mathrm{Cl}(V_{10})$ is antisymmetrisation, $q(v_1\wedge v_2)=v_1v_2-(v_1,v_2)$ [ESW, (29)]. Applied to a two-form, such as $F_A$, the symbol $\rho$ means $\rho\circ q$, as in $\rho(F_A)$ [ESW, (33)].

• $d$ is the exterior derivative along $\mathbb R^4$; every field is constant along $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$. The operator $d^*$ is the formal adjoint of $d$ for the Euclidean metric, $\mathrm{dvol}$ is the Euclidean volume form of $\mathbb R^4$, and ${\not d}=\rho\circ d$ is the Dirac operator $\Gamma(\Sigma)\to\Gamma(\Sigma^*)$ [ESW, §2.1]; the same formula on $\Sigma^*$-valued functions is written ${\not d}|_{\Sigma^*}$.

Fix an orientation of $V$ and let $\mathrm{dvol}$ also denote the corresponding four-form on $V$. Then $\rho(q(\mathrm{dvol}))$ squares to $1$ on $\Sigma$ and on $\Sigma^*$, with eigenvalues $+1$ and $-1$ each of multiplicity $8$. Writing

Let $v_1,\dots,v_4$ be an oriented orthonormal basis of $V$, so $q(\mathrm{dvol})=v_1v_2v_3v_4$ in $\mathrm{Cl}(V_{10})$. By the Clifford relation the $v_i$ anticommute pairwise and square to $1$, hence

For $v=v_1$, moving $v_1$ through $v_1v_2v_3v_4$ meets $v_2,v_3,v_4$ once each, so $v_1\,(v_1v_2v_3v_4)=-(v_1v_2v_3v_4)\,v_1$; the same holds for every $v\in V$ by linearity. For $w\in W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$, $w$ anticommutes with all four $v_i$, so $w\,(v_1v_2v_3v_4)=(+1)(v_1v_2v_3v_4)\,w$. Since $\rho(v)$ maps $\Sigma\to\Sigma^*$, the first relation reads $\rho(v)\rho(q(\mathrm{dvol}))|_{\Sigma}=-\rho(q(\mathrm{dvol}))|_{\Sigma^*}\rho(v)$, so $\rho(v)$ maps the $+1$ eigenspace on $\Sigma$ to the $-1$ eigenspace on $\Sigma^*$; the second relation gives $\rho(w)$ mapping the $+1$ eigenspace on $\Sigma$ to the $+1$ eigenspace on $\Sigma^*$. For the multiplicities, pick a unit vector $w\in W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$. The even element $v_1w$ satisfies $(v_1w)^2=-v_1^2w^2=-1$ and $v_1w\,(v_1v_2v_3v_4)=-(v_1v_2v_3v_4)\,v_1w$, so $\rho(v_1w)$ is an invertible endomorphism of $\Sigma$ (and of $\Sigma^*$) exchanging the two eigenspaces of $\rho(q(\mathrm{dvol}))$; hence each eigenspace has dimension $16/2=8$. ∎

The names of the eigenspaces depend on the orientation of $V$; the opposite orientation exchanges $S_+\leftrightarrow S_-$ in all four of them. This choice is a convention of the program, fixed once and used in Chapter 2 to name the supercharges.

The component of $A$ along $V$ is the connection $A|_V$, the component along $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ is $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$, and $\iota_wA=A(w)$ for $w\in W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ are the six scalars. We write $\mathscr E_c$ for the compactly supported elements of $\mathscr E$.

The degrees are those of [ESW, Rem 1.33]: the ghost $c$ is a section in degree $-1$, which forces $A^*$ in degree $+1$ and $c^*$ in degree $+2$. Signs follow the Koszul rule for the total parity, the sum of the $\mathbb Z$-degree and the $\mathbb Z/2$-degree modulo $2$ [ESW, §1.1].

For each of the three pairs, call the member of even total parity the even member: $A$, $\lambda^*$, $c^*$; their partners $A^*$, $\lambda$, $c$ are odd. Every pairing in [(1.1)](#b-00058) is read with its left entry first, as printed in [ESW, (31)]. In [ESW] the full action is $S$ and the interaction is $I$; in [C07] the letter $S$ denotes the interaction. Here $S$ is always the full action and $I$ the interaction.

With the coefficient $-\tfrac14$ in front of the Hodge pairing $(F_A,F_A)$, the identity $\{S,S^{(1)}(Q_1)\}=0$ of [ESW, Lemma 3.4] holds. With $+\tfrac14$, or with $-\tfrac12$ (the reading of $(F_A,F_A)$ as a sum over ordered pairs of directions, which doubles the Hodge pairing), it fails, already for abelian $\mathfrak g$ on the quadratic part of the action.

Let $a$ be the coefficient of $(F_A,F_A)$. For abelian $\mathfrak g$ the bracket $\{S,S^{(1)}(Q_1)\}$ is affine in $a$: the term $a(dA,dA)$ meets $-(\Gamma(Q_1,\lambda),A^*)$ through the $(A,A^*)$ pair, $\tfrac12(\lambda,{\not d}\lambda)$ meets $\tfrac12(\rho(dA)Q_1,\lambda^*)$ through the $(\lambda^*,\lambda)$ pair, and $(dc,A^*)$ meets $\tfrac12(\rho(dA)Q_1,\lambda^*)$ in $(\rho(d\,dc)Q_1,\lambda^*)=0$. The explicit evaluation of this affine function, as a local functional modulo total derivatives, gives zero at $a=-\tfrac14$ and a nonzero functional at $a=+\tfrac14$ and at $a=-\tfrac12$; hence $a=-\tfrac14$ is its unique zero. For $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(2)$, $a=-\tfrac14$ and two sampled $Q_1\in\Sigma$ with small Gaussian-integer components, the density of $\{S,S^{(1)}(Q_1)\}$, a polynomial in the jets of all fields, has identically vanishing Euler–Lagrange derivatives, so the local functional vanishes. For general $\mathfrak g$ the identity is [ESW, Lemma 3.4] in ten dimensions, pulled back along the reduction [ESW, Prop 2.20]. ∎

The vertex function is the coefficient of the product of the $r_j$ of the odd legs, in leg order, in the part multilinear in the legs, with the factor $(2\pi)^4\delta(\sum_jp_j)$ removed.

Write $S=\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle+I$. Both summands are even, so by graded symmetry $\{I,\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle\}=\{\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle,I\}=QI$ (Proposition [1.11](#b-00083)), and

The first term is $Q$ applied to $\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle$; by the preservation of the pairing in Proposition [1.11](#b-00083), $\langle Qe,Qe\rangle=-(-1)^{|e|}\langle e,Q^2e\rangle$, so this term is a multiple of $\langle e,Q^2e\rangle$ and vanishes by $Q^2=0$. This gives the equivalence of the first two items.

Explicit evaluation. Take $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(2)$ with an invariant pairing positive definite on the compact real form. The density of $\{S,S\}$, computed from Definitions [1.5](#b-00041)–[1.8](#b-00056) as a polynomial in the jets of all six fields with exact rational arithmetic, has identically vanishing Euler–Lagrange derivatives with respect to every field; hence $\{S,S\}=0$ as a local functional. The same holds separately for $\{\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle,\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle\}$ and for $2QI+\{I,I\}$, while $QI\neq0$. For each of the three other relative sign patterns of the $(\lambda^*,\lambda)$ and $(c^*,c)$ pairings, and for the reversed sign of $\tfrac12([c,c],c^*)$, the same computation gives a density with a nonvanishing Euler–Lagrange derivative.

General $\mathfrak g$. The action [(1.1)](#b-00058) is the BV action of the BRST theory of [ESW, Def 3.2], built as in [ESW, Def 1.34] with the natural pairing of the shifted cotangent bundle; it satisfies $\{S,S\}=0$ for every $\mathfrak g$, and the dimensional reduction preserves it [ESW, Def 1.55, Prop 1.56]. The natural pairing differs from Definition [1.5](#b-00041) at most by a sign on each of the three pairs, and these signs are independent of $\mathfrak g$. An overall sign leaves $\{S,S\}=0$ invariant, and by the explicit evaluation the pattern of Definition [1.5](#b-00041) is the unique one among the four relative patterns with $\{S,S\}=0$ for $\mathfrak{su}(2)$. Hence the natural pairing coincides with Definition [1.5](#b-00041) up to an overall sign, and $\{S,S\}=0$ holds for every $\mathfrak g$. ∎
Decompose $\{S,S\}$ by the number of antifields. Each term is a product of a derivative along a field and a derivative along its partner, weighted by the sign of that pair.

• No antifield: the gauge variation of $\int\mathrm{dvol}\big(-\tfrac14(F_A,F_A)+\tfrac12(\lambda,{\not d}_A\lambda)\big)$ under $A\mapsto d_Ac$, $\lambda\mapsto[c,\lambda]$. The $A$-variation enters through the $(A,A^*)$ pair and the $\lambda$-variation through the $(\lambda^*,\lambda)$ pair; gauge invariance cancels them for one relative sign of these two pairs.

The dilatation of a composite operator, and every other superconformal transformation, acts on the fields of $\mathcal N=4$ super Yang–Mills theory up to gauge transformations and equations of motion. In the BV formalism this structure is a Maurer–Cartan element of a Chevalley–Eilenberg complex, an $L_\infty$ action in the sense of [ESW, Def 1.26–1.27], and it is the classical input of the equivariant observables used later. [ESW, (32)–(34), Thm 3.3] construct it for the Poincaré supersymmetry algebra; the special conformal transformations and the special supercharges require Weyl weights, a compensating term with the six scalars, and an R-symmetry rotation in the odd bracket. This chapter realises $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$ on Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$, fixes the sign conventions of the complex, writes the action $S+S^{(1)}+S^{(2)}$, and states which components of its master equation hold for every gauge algebra and which were evaluated.

Throughout, $x\in V$ denotes the position on $\mathbb R^4$ and $E$ the Euler vector field $E(x)=x$ of [SW, (3)]; in this chapter $E$ always means this vector field. In arity $n\ge5$ every term contains $S^{(k)}$ with $k\ge3$ or $\{S^{(k)},S^{(l)}\}$ with $k+l=n$, hence $k\ge3$ or $l\ge3$, and vanishes. In arity $3$ with at most one odd argument, every term contains $S^{(2)}$ with an even entry, because among $[x_i,x_j]$ and $x_k$, and among any two of the arguments, at most one entry is odd; so every term vanishes. In arity $3$ with three odd arguments, every $[x_i,x_j]$ is even, so the equation of Lemma [2.11](#b-00225) reduces to the cyclic sum $\sum_{\rm cyc}\{S^{(1)}(x_1),S^{(2)}(x_2,x_3)\}$. No derivative acts on the spinors, so the cyclic sum is computed pointwise in $x$ exactly as in the proof of [ESW, Lemma 3.7], with $Q_1,Q_2,Q_3$ replaced by the values of the three conformal Killing spinors at $x$; it vanishes by [ESW, Assumption 3.1], which holds for $\Sigma$ the ten-dimensional semi-spin representation [ESW, §3.1], and the Clifford relation. ∎

Let $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(2)$, with $(-,-)$ equal to $-\tfrac12$ times the trace form $\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}\,\mathrm{ad})$. Costello's renormalisation needs a gauge-fixing operator $Q^{GF}$, the heat kernel of $H=[Q,Q^{GF}]$ and the propagator $P(\varepsilon,T)$, and its axioms [C07, Def 4.3.3] are formulated on a compact manifold; [C07, §5.2] records that Yang–Mills theory in second-order form lies outside them. On Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$ we keep a single regulator, the lower Schwinger limit $\varepsilon$, set the upper limit to $\infty$, and introduce no infrared scale. This chapter constructs a Feynman-gauge operator $Q^{GF}$ that satisfies three of the five axioms, identifies the two that fail, and proves the identities that hold with these data: $QP(\varepsilon,\infty)=K_\varepsilon$, the UV-boundary identity, the acyclicity of $Q$ at scale $\infty$, and the one-loop formula for the graph expansion.

At scale $\infty$ the differential on functionals is $d_{CE}+Q$ ($\Delta_\infty=0$, $\{-,-\}_\infty=0$), and Corollary [3.17](#b-00430) shows that $Q$ alone has trivial cohomology on functionals without constant term: every $Q$-closed functional at scale $\infty$ is $Q$-exact, so an arbitrary functional $O(\varepsilon)$ produces a class that carries no information. The content of an operator is the local functional $O(\varepsilon)$ at the UV end whose flow to scale $\infty$ has an $\varepsilon\to0$ limit. This requirement fixes the singular part of $O(\varepsilon)$ uniquely; the finite part is the scheme freedom. Correspondingly, an equation $Q\,O[\infty]=Y[\infty]$ between observables at scale $\infty$ has content because $Y$ is required to be local, and anomalous dimensions are classes in the cohomology of local functionals.
